questions.prompt: VNet A peers with B, and B peers with C. No direct A–C peering or transit routing is configured. What should be expected?

options.text: A and C do not gain connectivity merely from these two peerings.
A and C automatically connect through B.
options.explanation: A hub connection alone does not create transit routing.

options.text: A–C connectivity appears after changing only the peering names.
options.explanation: Names do not create network paths.

options.text: A and C share one address space automatically.
options.explanation: Peering does not merge or renumber their address spaces.

questions.prompt: A spoke without its own gateway must use a supported VPN gateway in a peered hub. Which TWO peering settings are required on the respective sides?

options.text: Allow gateway transit on the hub-side peering
options.explanation: The hub permits use of its gateway.

options.text: Use remote gateways on the spoke-side peering
options.explanation: The spoke chooses to use the permitted remote gateway.

options.text: Use remote gateways on every spoke peering simultaneously
options.explanation: A VNet can use a remote gateway through only one peering.

options.text: Only allow forwarded traffic and omit both gateway settings
options.explanation: Forwarded traffic permission alone does not configure gateway transit.

questions.prompt: What does enabling Allow forwarded traffic on a VNet peering do?

options.text: Permit eligible traffic forwarded through the peered network.
options.explanation: The setting allows forwarded packets but does not build their routing path.

options.text: Automatically create an NVA and all required UDRs.
options.explanation: Those resources and routes must be configured separately.

options.text: Automatically share every private DNS zone.
options.explanation: DNS configuration is separate from forwarded traffic permission.

options.text: Remove NSG filtering from the connection.
